notes: Every resource needs a working source URL and a lastChecked date. Case studies use one template: region, what, how, impact, limitation. Topics: energy, data-centres, hardware, ai, nature, oceans, climate, policy, water.

resources.title: DeepMind and Google data-centre cooling
resources.what: AI that runs data-centre cooling more efficiently
resources.how: A machine-learning system trained on historical sensor data predicts how hot the data centre will get and recommends cooling settings, so cooling is not over-provisioned.
resources.impact: In tests it cut the energy used for cooling by up to 40%, which Google said equalled a 15% cut in overall energy overhead (PUE).
resources.limitation: Results come from Google's own facilities and were reported by Google, not independently measured.

resources.title: How much electricity do data centres use?
resources.what: The International Energy Agency's estimate of data-centre electricity demand, driven partly by AI
resources.how: The IEA models data-centre demand from server shipments, utilisation and efficiency trends, and publishes scenarios to 2030 and 2035.
resources.impact: Data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of global electricity. In the IEA's base case this roughly doubles to about 945 TWh by 2030.
resources.limitation: These are projections with wide uncertainty; the IEA's own range for 2035 spans 700 to 1,700 TWh.

resources.title: Data centres' growing share of US electricity
resources.what: A US Department of Energy-backed estimate of data-centre electricity use
resources.how: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory combines equipment stock, usage and efficiency data to estimate consumption and project it forward.
resources.impact: Data centres used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 (176 TWh) and could reach 6.7% to 12% by 2028.
resources.limitation: The 2028 figure is a range because it depends on how fast AI servers are installed and how efficient they are.

source.name: US Department of Energy (Berkeley Lab report)

resources.title: Measuring a language model's carbon footprint: BLOOM
resources.what: A full life-cycle estimate of the emissions from training the open BLOOM language model
resources.how: The researchers counted the electricity used in training, the grid's carbon intensity, idle power, and the emissions from manufacturing the hardware.
resources.impact: Final training emitted about 24.7 tonnes of CO2e from dynamic power alone, and about 50.5 tonnes when equipment manufacturing and other operations were included.
resources.limitation: France's grid is low-carbon, so the same training elsewhere would likely emit more; the study also excludes later use of the model.

resources.title: Rainforest Connection: listening for illegal logging
resources.region: Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Romania and others
resources.what: Acoustic monitoring that alerts rangers to illegal logging in real time
resources.how: Recycled, solar-powered phones hidden in trees stream forest audio to the cloud, where a TensorFlow model listens for chainsaws and logging trucks and sends alerts to rangers' phones.
resources.impact: Gives local forest guardians, starting with the Tembé people in Brazil, a way to respond while logging is happening rather than after.
resources.limitation: It needs mobile coverage and people on the ground who can safely respond to alerts.
resources.correction: The old site called this Google's Project Loon. Loon was an internet-balloon project; the chainsaw detection is Rainforest Connection's work.

resources.title: PAWS: predicting poaching hotspots
resources.what: An AI tool that helps rangers decide where to patrol
resources.how: PAWS splits a park into 1 km squares and uses past patrol records, terrain and distance to roads to rate each square's poaching risk.
resources.impact: In field tests, rangers following PAWS removed a whole roll of elephant snares, and 10 antelope snares before any animals were caught.
resources.limitation: Predictions are only as good as past patrol data, which is patchy in areas rangers rarely visit.

resources.title: Global Fishing Watch
resources.what: A free public map of industrial fishing activity
resources.how: Machine learning classifies ships' position signals (AIS) to tell when and where vessels are fishing, using Google's cloud and Earth Engine.
resources.impact: Lets governments, researchers and the public see fishing activity, including in protected areas.
resources.limitation: It relies on ships broadcasting their position, and some vessels switch their transponders off.

resources.title: Wild Me and Microsoft AI for Earth
resources.what: Computer vision that identifies individual animals from photos
resources.how: Wildbook, Wild Me's open-source platform, matches the unique spot and stripe patterns of animals such as whale sharks in photos from researchers and the public.
resources.impact: Helps scientists count and track endangered populations without tagging animals. Wild Me joined Microsoft's AI for Earth programme in 2018.
resources.limitation: It depends on enough good photos being submitted, so coverage varies a lot by species and place.

resources.title: Plantix: diagnosing crop disease from a photo
resources.what: A free app that identifies plant pests, diseases and nutrient problems
resources.how: Farmers photograph a sick plant; an image-recognition model trained on photos labelled by crop scientists suggests a diagnosis and treatment.
resources.impact: Can help farmers act sooner and use treatments more precisely. Most reported impact figures come from user surveys.
resources.limitation: Diagnoses depend on photo quality and on the crops and diseases in its database.

resources.title: IBM Green Horizons: forecasting air pollution
resources.what: Machine-learning air pollution forecasts built with Beijing's environmental protection bureau
resources.how: The system combines weather data, pollution sensor readings and traffic and industry information to forecast pollution levels.
resources.impact: In 2015 it was reported to forecast pollution across Beijing up to 72 hours ahead, to help officials plan measures such as limiting traffic.
resources.limitation: Most results were reported by IBM in 2015 and 2016; its later use and impact are not documented here.

resources.title: CarbonPlan: checking carbon removal claims
resources.what: A nonprofit that publishes open data and analysis on carbon removal and offsets
resources.how: It reviews carbon removal projects and offset programmes with open-source tools and publishes its methods so others can check them.
resources.impact: Helps companies and policymakers judge which climate claims are credible.
resources.limitation: This is data science and transparency work rather than AI; it is here because good measurement matters as much as clever models.

resources.title: Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning
resources.authors: David Rolnick, Priya Donti, Lynn Kaack and others (including Andrew Ng, Demis Hassabis and Yoshua Bengio)
resources.summary: A broad map of where machine learning can help on climate, from power grids and buildings to farming and disaster response.
resources.why: The best single starting point for seeing where AI can and cannot help with climate change.
resources.readingTime: Long read: dip into the sections you need

resources.title: Energy and Policy Considerations for Deep Learning in NLP
resources.authors: Emma Strubell, Ananya Ganesh and Andrew McCallum
resources.summary: Estimates the energy use and emissions of training several language models, including tuning and architecture search.
resources.why: One of the first papers to make AI's training footprint visible; its largest estimate is an upper-end case, and later work has refined the numbers.

resources.title: The real climate and transformative impact of ICT
resources.authors: Charlotte Freitag, Mike Berners-Lee and others
resources.summary: Reviews estimates of the ICT sector's emissions and argues they are often too low because supply chains are not fully counted.
resources.why: Explains why tech's share of global emissions is likely 2.1% to 3.9%, and why efficiency alone has not reduced it.

resources.title: Estimating the Carbon Footprint of BLOOM, a 176B Parameter Language Model
resources.authors: Alexandra Sasha Luccioni, Sylvain Viguier and Anne-Laure Ligozat
resources.summary: Measures the full life-cycle emissions of training and running a large open language model.
resources.why: Shows how to count hardware and idle power, not just training electricity, which roughly doubles the total.

resources.title: Robustness of AI-based weather forecasts in a changing climate
resources.authors: Thomas Rackow and others (ECMWF and AWI)
resources.summary: Tests three AI weather models on a pre-industrial year, the present day and a world 2.9 K warmer.
resources.why: AI forecasts stay skilful, but drift back toward the climate they were trained on, so they need care when used for future climates.

resources.title: Climate-Invariant Machine Learning
resources.summary: Builds physical knowledge into machine-learning climate models so they keep working in warmer climates than the ones they were trained on.
resources.why: A key step toward AI climate models we can trust outside their training data.
